claim: Cultured meat is an innovative and emerging technique that produces meat directly from cell cultures.
source: Cultured meat is an innovative and emerging technique that produces meat directly from cell cultures, potentially providing a high-quality, safe, and stable source of animal protein (Chriki and Hocquette, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chriki and Hocquette, 2020

claim: Cultured meat generates fewer greenhouse gases compared to traditional livestock and poultry farming.
source: In comparison to traditional livestock and poultry farming, cultured meat generates fewer greenhouse gases, utilizes less arable land, and causes less animal harm (Mattick et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mattick et al., 2015

claim: Cultured meat utilizes less arable land compared to traditional livestock and poultry farming.
source: In comparison to traditional livestock and poultry farming, cultured meat generates fewer greenhouse gases, utilizes less arable land, and causes less animal harm (Mattick et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mattick et al., 2015

claim: Cultured meat causes less animal harm compared to traditional livestock and poultry farming.
source: In comparison to traditional livestock and poultry farming, cultured meat generates fewer greenhouse gases, utilizes less arable land, and causes less animal harm (Mattick et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mattick et al., 2015

claim: Stem cells like muscle stem cells and pluripotent stem cells have frequently been utilized as the cellular source for cultured meat.
source: While the stem cells like muscle stem cells and pluripotent stem cells have frequently been utilized as the cellular source for cultured meat, these stem cells are rare in the animal body and difficult to obtain and amplify on a large scale.
evidence: Statement of established practice in the field

claim: Muscle stem cells and pluripotent stem cells are rare in the animal body and difficult to obtain and amplify on a large scale.
source: While the stem cells like muscle stem cells and pluripotent stem cells have frequently been utilized as the cellular source for cultured meat, these stem cells are rare in the animal body and difficult to obtain and amplify on a large scale.
evidence: Statement based on established biological knowledge

claim: Somatic cells could be efficiently converted into muscle cells under certain conditions.
source: In contrast, the somatic cells, which constitute the body, could be efficiently converted into muscle cells under certain conditions.
evidence: General statement supported by subsequent citations and experimental data in the manuscript

claim: Fibroblasts can replicate indefinitely in vitro.
source: The fibroblasts can replicate indefinitely in vitro and are amenable to myogenesis, adipogenesis, and chondrogenesis (French et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2010), which produce muscle, fat, and extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins that constitute the meat and the associated texture and flavor.
evidence: Supported by citations to French et al., 2004 and Yin et al., 2010

claim: Fibroblasts are amenable to myogenesis, adipogenesis, and chondrogenesis.
source: The fibroblasts can replicate indefinitely in vitro and are amenable to myogenesis, adipogenesis, and chondrogenesis (French et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2010), which produce muscle, fat, and extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins that constitute the meat and the associated texture and flavor.
evidence: Supported by citations to French et al., 2004 and Yin et al., 2010

claim: Fibroblast cells from farm animals have been utilized as the source cells for cultured meat production.
source: Recently, the fibroblast cells from farm animals have been utilized as the source cells for cultured meat production, with or without myogenesis (Jeong et al., 2022; Pasitka et al., 2023), demonstrating the feasibility of somatic cell-derived seed cells as a sustainable and ethical option for cultured meat production.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jeong et al., 2022 and Pasitka et al., 2023

claim: A protocol for the controlled transdifferentiation of chicken fibroblasts into myoblasts has been previously developed.
source: We have previously developed a protocol for the controlled transdifferentiation of chicken fibroblasts into myoblasts, which subsequently form multinucleated myotubes and express mature muscle proteins (Ren et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ren et al., 2022

claim: Chicken fibroblasts can be efficiently converted into fat-depositing lipocytes by treating them with chicken serum medium.
source: Moreover, chicken fibroblasts could also be efficiently converted into fat-depositing lipocytes by treating them with chicken serum (CS) medium or other substances such as fatty acids (Hausman, 2012; Kim et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hausman, 2012; Kim et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021

claim: Chicken fibroblasts can be efficiently converted into fat-depositing lipocytes by treating them with fatty acids.
source: Moreover, chicken fibroblasts could also be efficiently converted into fat-depositing lipocytes by treating them with chicken serum (CS) medium or other substances such as fatty acids (Hausman, 2012; Kim et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hausman, 2012; Kim et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021

claim: Chicken fibroblasts were able to proliferate normally at 6, 3, and 1.5% serum concentrations, but at decreasing rates.
source: The results showed that the cells were able to proliferate normally at 6, 3, and 1.5% serum concentrations, but at decreasing rates as shown by the EdU assay (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in EdU assay results in Figure 1A and B

claim: Chicken fibroblasts could proliferate stably in 1% chicken serum.
source: The results showed that chicken fibroblasts could proliferate stably in the 1% CS (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and the cell populations multiplied three times in 3 d as demonstrated by the CCK-8 assay (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and CCK-8 assay in Figure 1C

claim: Cell populations in 1% chicken serum multiplied three times in 3 days.
source: The results showed that chicken fibroblasts could proliferate stably in the 1% CS (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and the cell populations multiplied three times in 3 d as demonstrated by the CCK-8 assay (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 assay data shown in Figure 1C

claim: GelMA hydrogel can form a stable and porous structure for cell implantation.
source: GelMA hydrogel can form a stable and porous structure for cell implantation and is commonly used in tissue engineering because of its great biocompatibility and mechanical tenability (Pepelanova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pepelanova et al., 2018

claim: GelMA hydrogel is commonly used in tissue engineering because of its great biocompatibility and mechanical tenability.
source: GelMA hydrogel can form a stable and porous structure for cell implantation and is commonly used in tissue engineering because of its great biocompatibility and mechanical tenability (Pepelanova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pepelanova et al., 2018

claim: The porosity of GelMA hydrogels at 3, 5, 7, and 9wt% was measured to be 83.27, 65.01, 62.47, and 57.96%, respectively.
source: The porosity was measured to be 83.27, 65.01, 62.47, and 57.96%, respectively.
evidence: Direct measurement data from the experiment

claim: The higher the mass concentration of hydrogels, the tighter the 3D mesh structure formed and the smaller the porosity.
source: Thus, the higher the mass concentration of hydrogels, the tighter the 3D mesh structure formed and the smaller the porosity (Figure 2A).
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The pore diameters in the scaffolds ranged from 3 µm2 to 100 µm2.
source: The pore diameters in the scaffolds were determined to range from 3 µm2 to 100 µm2, showing the biggest pore size in 3% hydrogel and the smallest in 9% hydrogel (Figure 2B).
evidence: Measurement data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The 3% hydrogel collapsed in the medium 2 days after cell implantation.
source: However, the 3% hydrogel collapsed in the medium 2 d after cell implantation and thus did not support the long-term cell growth.
evidence: Experimental observation during the study

claim: Cells successfully propagated in 5, 7, and 9% hydrogels for the entire duration of the 9-day experiment.
source: We continued to monitor the 3D cell proliferation and found that the cells successfully propagated in 5, 7, and 9% hydrogels for the entire duration of the experiment.
evidence: Experimental observation over 9 days

claim: The 5% concentration hydrogel was found to be the best option for cell attachment and growth.
source: Among the tested hydrogels, the 5% concentration was found to be the best option for cell attachment and growth as shown by the densest cellular structure formed, and thus be utilized for the subsequent analysis.
evidence: Comparative analysis of different hydrogel concentrations

claim: By the ninth day, cells in 3D culture multiplied more than 15 times.
source: By the fifth day, most of the cells were elongated with irregular shape and short tentacles and packed tightly, and by the ninth day they multiplied more than 15 times and formed dense fibrous bundles (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Quantitative data from PKH26 fluorescent labeling shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: The proliferation efficiency of chicken fibroblast cells gradually increased over time in 3D culture and reached replication levels even higher than those in 2D culture.
source: The proliferation efficiency of chicken fibroblast cells gradually increased over time in 3D culture and reached replication levels even higher than those in 2D culture (Figures 1B and 2E,F).
evidence: Comparative EdU assay data shown in Figures 1B and 2E,F

claim: 3D culture conditions provide a more favorable environment for cell growth than 2D culture.
source: This result indicates that 3D culture conditions provide a more favorable environment for cell growth.
evidence: Inference from proliferation data comparing 2D and 3D cultures

claim: Elongated multinucleated myotubes and abundant expression of myosin heavy chain were observed after 3 days of myogenic induction.
source: We observed elongated multinucleated myotubes and abundant expression of myosin heavy chain (MHC) after 3 d of myogenic induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B

claim: Reducing serum concentrations did not increase myotube formation but instead caused massive cell death.
source: However, we found that reducing serum concentrations did not increase the myotube formation but instead caused massive cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: A simple MyoD overexpression strategy is sufficient for efficient production of mature muscle cells in chicken fibroblasts.
source: Therefore, it seems that the 'serum deprivation' could not further improve the myogenic transdifferentiation in chicken fibroblast cells and a simple MyoD overexpression strategy is sufficient for efficient production of mature muscle cells.
evidence: Inference from experimental results comparing different serum conditions

claim: Abundant multinucleate MHC+ myotubes were identified at multiple focal planes within the gel.
source: We identified abundant multinucleate MHC+ myotubes at multiple focal planes within the gel (Figure 3B, Figure 3—video 1), indicating successful myogenic transdifferentiation of 3D cultured chicken fibroblasts.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—video 1

claim: The myotube formation efficiency (fusion index) in 3D reached 30.49%, which was significantly higher than that of the 2D under the same transdifferentiation conditions.
source: The myotube formation efficiency (fusion index) in 3D reached 30.49%, which was significantly higher than that of the 2D under the same transdifferentiation conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantitative comparison data shown in Figure 3C

claim: MyoG, MYH6, and MCK significantly increased upon transdifferentiation in both 2D and 3D.
source: All myogenic factors, including MyoG, MYH6, and MCK, significantly increased upon transdifferentiation in both 2D and 3D.
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3F

claim: The transdifferentiated cells exhibited significantly higher expression of MyoG and MCK in 3D conditions compared to that in 2D.
source: In addition, the transdifferentiated cells exhibited significantly higher expression of MyoG and MCK in 3D conditions compared to that in 2D, indicating more robust myogenic differentiation and maturation of cells in the 3D microenvironment.
evidence: RT-qPCR data comparing 2D and 3D shown in Figure 3F

claim: The muscle-specific intermediate filament Desmin was expressed only in the MyoD-transdifferentiated cells, but not in the original fibroblasts or the embryonic skin-derived myofibroblasts.
source: The immunofluorescence staining of 3D cultured cells showed that the muscle-specific intermediate filament Desmin (Paulin and Li, 2004) was expressed only in the MyoD-transdifferentiated cells, but not in the original fibroblasts or the embryonic skin-derived myofibroblasts (Figure 4A).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A with citation to Paulin and Li, 2004

claim: The classical myofibroblast marker alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) was expressed only in myofibroblasts, but not in the fibroblast or the transdifferentiated cells.
source: In contrast, the classical myofibroblast marker alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) (Hinz et al., 2007) was expressed only in myofibroblasts, but not in the fibroblast or the transdifferentiated cells (Figure 4).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B with citation to Hinz et al., 2007

claim: The fibroblast intermediate filament Vimentin was abundantly expressed in the fibroblasts but reduced in the myogenic transdifferentiated cells.
source: The fibroblast intermediate filament Vimentin (Tarbit et al., 2019) was abundantly expressed in the fibroblasts but reduced in the myogenic transdifferentiated cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C with citation to Tarbit et al., 2019

claim: After myogenic induction in 3D, the skeletal muscle-specific genes Desmin and Six1 were significantly elevated.
source: Furthermore, the RT-qPCR showed that, after myogenic induction in 3D, the skeletal muscle-specific genes Desmin and Six1 (Relaix et al., 2013) were significantly elevated (Figure 4D), whereas the fibroblast gene Thy-1 was significantly reduced (Figure 4E).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D with citation to Relaix et al., 2013

claim: The fibroblast gene Thy-1 was significantly reduced after myogenic induction in 3D.
source: Furthermore, the RT-qPCR showed that, after myogenic induction in 3D, the skeletal muscle-specific genes Desmin and Six1 (Relaix et al., 2013) were significantly elevated (Figure 4D), whereas the fibroblast gene Thy-1 was significantly reduced (Figure 4E).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The expression of core TGFβ signaling components, TGFβ-1, TGFβ-3, and Smad3, remained unchanged during the transdifferentiation process.
source: We found that the expression of core TGFβ signaling components, TGFβ-1, TGFβ-3, and Smad3, remained unchanged during the transdifferentiation process (Figure 4F), indicating that the classical myofibroblast lineage was not induced.
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4F

claim: The 8 µg/ml fatty acids plus 60 µg/ml insulin can induce lipogenesis most efficiently in 2D chicken fibroblasts.
source: After extensive optimization of the concentrations of supplements in the medium, we identified that the 8 µg/ml fatty acids plus 60 µg/ml insulin (abbreviated as FI, F: fatty acids, I: insulin) can induce lipogenesis most efficiently in 2D chicken fibroblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Optimization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: Extensive Oil Red O signal was found inside the hydrogel matrix at different focal planes after lipogenic induction.
source: We found extensive Oil Red O signal inside the hydrogel matrix at different focal planes and the lipid droplets were clearly visible as beaded strings under magnification (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 5B, C, and Figure 5—video 1

claim: The expression of genes involved in lipogenesis and triglyceride synthesis was significantly higher in the cells with lipogenic stimulation compared to the control.
source: The RT-qPCR analysis illustrated the expression of genes involved in lipogenesis and triglyceride synthesis was significantly higher in the cells with lipogenic stimulation compared to the control (Figure 5D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The genes encoding for PPARγ, Gpd1, and FABP4 all showed higher expression in 3D than that in 2D upon lipogenic stimulation.
source: Notably, the genes encoding for PPARγ (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma), Gpd1 (glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase), and FABP4 (fatty acid binding protein 4) all showed higher expression in 3D than that in 2D.
evidence: RT-qPCR comparison data between 2D and 3D shown in Figure 5D

claim: The expression of Znf423 only increased upon lipogenic induction in 3D but not in 2D conditions.
source: Interestingly, the expression of Znf423 (zinc finger protein 423), which is a PPARγ transcriptional activator (Addison et al., 2014; Longo et al., 2018), only increased upon lipogenic induction in 3D but not in 2D conditions.
evidence: RT-qPCR data with citations to Addison et al., 2014 and Longo et al., 2018

claim: Cells grown in 3D hydrogel showed enhanced lipogenesis compared to the flat surface cultured cells.
source: It seems that the cells grown in 3D hydrogel showed enhanced lipogenesis compared to the flat surface cultured cells, similar to the myogenic transdifferentiation process in 3D.
evidence: Inference from comparative gene expression data between 2D and 3D

claim: Chicken serum alone could stimulate fat accumulation effectively.
source: Our results showed that the CS alone could also stimulate fat accumulation effectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: The lipogenic induction increased the triglyceride significantly in the cell matrix.
source: We further measured the triglyceride content and found that the lipogenic induction increased the triglyceride significantly in the cell matrix (Figure 5E).
evidence: Triglyceride measurement data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Plenty of MHC+ myotubes and Oil Red O-stained lipids were found to intermingle after the myogenic/lipogenic treatment in 2D conditions.
source: In 2D conditions, plenty of MHC+ myotubes and Oil Red O-stained lipids were found to intermingle after the myogenic/lipogenic treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and some of the red marked lipid droplets were located inside the myotubes, indicating that the transformed muscle cells indeed deposit fat autonomously to constitute intramyocellular lipids (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Some lipid droplets were located inside the myotubes, indicating that the transformed muscle cells deposit fat autonomously to constitute intramyocellular lipids.
source: In 2D conditions, plenty of MHC+ myotubes and Oil Red O-stained lipids were found to intermingle after the myogenic/lipogenic treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and some of the red marked lipid droplets were located inside the myotubes, indicating that the transformed muscle cells indeed deposit fat autonomously to constitute intramyocellular lipids (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Oil Red O-labeled lipid droplets were mixed with the densely packed MHC+ myotubes in 3D hydrogel.
source: Next, we applied similar treatment to the cells cultured in 3D hydrogel and also identified Oil Red O-labeled lipid droplets mixed with the densely packed MHC+ myotubes (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence and Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: The induced cells showed significantly higher expression of genes involved in both myogenesis and lipogenesis compared to the control 3D cells without myogenic/lipogenic stimulations.
source: Compared to the control 3D cells without myogenic/lipogenic stimulations, the induced cells showed significantly higher expression of genes involved in both myogenesis and lipogenesis (Figure 6D).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D

claim: The extent of gene upregulation upon the combined myogenic/adipogenic stimulations was comparable to that of myogenic or adipogenic induction alone.
source: Interestingly, the extent of gene upregulation upon the combined myogenic/adipogenic stimulations was comparable to that of myogenic or adipogenic induction alone.
evidence: Comparative RT-qPCR data analysis

claim: Sequential myogenic transdifferentiation and lipid deposition do not interfere with each other when conducted in the same cells.
source: This finding suggests that sequential myogenic transdifferentiation and lipid deposition do not interfere with each other when conducted in the same cells.
evidence: Inference from gene expression data showing comparable upregulation

claim: The lipogenic stimulation in the 3D hydrogel cells increased the triglyceride content in the cultured meat to the levels comparable to or even higher than real chicken meat.
source: The results showed that the lipogenic stimulation in the 3D hydrogel cells increased the triglyceride content in the cultured meat to the levels comparable to or even higher than real chicken meat (Figure 6E).
evidence: Triglyceride measurement data comparing cultured meat to real chicken meat shown in Figure 6E

claim: The control cells without any induction or with only myogenic stimulation do not show apparent triglyceride accumulation.
source: In contrast, the control cells without any induction or with only myogenic stimulation do not show apparent triglyceride accumulation (Figure 6E).
evidence: Triglyceride measurement data shown in Figure 6E

claim: By fine-tuning the concentrations of insulin and fatty acids during lipogenic induction, the triglyceride contents in the final product of cultured meat can precisely reach any customized levels across the range from 1.5 mg/g to 7 mg/g.
source: By fine-tuning the concentrations of insulin and fatty acids during lipogenic induction, the triglyceride contents in the final product of cultured meat can precisely reach any customized levels across the range from 1.5 mg/g to 7 mg/g (Figure 6E), which overlap and surpass the levels in the fresh chicken breast and leg meat.
evidence: Experimental data showing dose-dependent triglyceride accumulation in Figure 6E

claim: The total collagen protein gradually increased and reached the plateau at 1.59 µg/mg in the final product.
source: We then examined the collagen content in the cultured meat and found that the total collagen protein gradually increased and reached the plateau at 1.59 µg/mg in the final product (Figure 7A).
evidence: Collagen measurement data shown in Figure 7A

claim: The expression of COL1A1 and COL1A2 gradually decreased during the time course of meat synthesis.
source: The expression of COL1A1 (collagen, type I, alpha 1) and COL1A2 (collagen, type I, alpha 2) gradually decreased, whereas the fibronectin increased during the time course of meat synthesis.
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Fibronectin expression increased during the time course of meat synthesis.
source: The expression of COL1A1 (collagen, type I, alpha 1) and COL1A2 (collagen, type I, alpha 2) gradually decreased, whereas the fibronectin increased during the time course of meat synthesis.
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The expression of elastin and laminin genes remained stable throughout the whole course of the experiment.
source: The expression of elastin and laminin genes remained stable throughout the whole course of the experiment (Figure 7B).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The laminin protein content was accumulated and increased steadily during 3D culturation.
source: However, the laminin protein content was accumulated and increased steadily during 3D culturation (Figure 7C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 7C

claim: The 3D+FI group clustered distinctly from the others in hierarchical clustering analysis.
source: The findings revealed that the 3D+FI group clustered distinctly from the others, while the 3D_MyoD and 3D_MyoD + FI groups exhibited greater similarity.
evidence: Hierarchical clustering analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 8B

claim: The 3D_MyoD and 3D_MyoD + FI groups exhibited greater similarity in hierarchical clustering analysis.
source: The findings revealed that the 3D+FI group clustered distinctly from the others, while the 3D_MyoD and 3D_MyoD + FI groups exhibited greater similarity.
evidence: Hierarchical clustering analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 8B

claim: The 3D_fibroblasts formed a distinct sub-cluster on their own in hierarchical clustering analysis.
source: Moreover, the 3D_fibroblasts formed a distinct sub-cluster on their own (Figure 8B), suggesting that myogenic or adipogenic transdifferentiation drives these cells away from their original fibroblastic state.
evidence: Hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 8B

claim: The majority (78%) of DEGs in the 3D_MyoD+FI are overlapped with 3D_MyoD and 3D+FI.
source: The results showed that the majority (78%) of DEGs in the 3D_MyoD+FI are overlapped with 3D_MyoD and 3D+FI, indicating that sequential myogenic/adipogenic induction in 3D_MyoD+FI is consistent with myogenic or adipogenic function individually (Figure 8D).
evidence: Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 8D

claim: Myogenic-specific pathways such as 'muscle organ development' were enriched in 3D_MyoD+FI cells.
source: In addition, the Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of upregulated DEGs in 3D_MyoD+FI cells confirmed that myogenic-specific pathways such as 'muscle organ development' and adipogenic-specific pathways such as 'PPAR signaling pathway' were enriched.
evidence: GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8F

claim: Adipogenic-specific pathways such as 'PPAR signaling pathway' were enriched in 3D_MyoD+FI cells.
source: In addition, the Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of upregulated DEGs in 3D_MyoD+FI cells confirmed that myogenic-specific pathways such as 'muscle organ development' and adipogenic-specific pathways such as 'PPAR signaling pathway' were enriched.
evidence: GO analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8F

claim: Several multifunctional signaling pathways such as 'JAK-STAT signaling pathway', 'NF-kappa B signaling pathway', and 'MAPK signaling pathway' were simultaneously activated during myogenic/adipogenic transdifferentiation.
source: In addition, we also identified several multifunctional signaling pathways such as 'JAK-STAT signaling pathway', 'NF-kappa B signaling pathway', and 'MAPK signaling pathway' that were simultaneously activated during myogenic/adipogenic transdifferentiation, which should have profound effects on both myogenesis (Bakkar and Guttridge, 2010; Jang and Baik, 2013; Keren et al., 2006) and adipogenesis (Batista et al., 2012; Bost et al., 2005; Richard and Stephens, 2011; Figure 8F).
evidence: GO analysis with multiple citations supporting the roles of these pathways

claim: High intramuscular fat contents can improve the cooking flavor and greatly increase the value of meat products.
source: In general, a very low level of intramuscular fat results in dry meat with a plain taste, whereas the high intramuscular fat contents can improve the cooking flavor and greatly increase the value of meat products, such as the high marbling beef from Japanese Wagyu cattle (Gotoh et al., 2018; Motoyama et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gotoh et al., 2018 and Motoyama et al., 2016

claim: Co-culturing pre-adipocytes with myoblasts may increase the intramuscular fat content, tenderness, and taste intensity of cultured meat.
source: For example, co-culturing pre-adipocytes with myoblasts may increase the intramuscular fat content, tenderness, and taste intensity of cultured meat (Lau et al., 1996; Pandurangan and Kim, 2015; Zagury et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lau et al., 1996; Pandurangan and Kim, 2015; Zagury et al., 2022

claim: Adipocytes growing near muscle cells can impair myogenesis.

claim: MyoD is the key myogenic transcription factor.

claim: Chicken fibroblasts could be converted into striated and elongated myotubes upon forced expression of MyoD.
source: The MyoD is the key myogenic transcription factor, and the chicken fibroblasts could be converted into striated and elongated myotubes (myofibers) upon forced expression of MyoD (Ren et al., 2022; Weintraub et al., 1989).

claim: The control chicken fibroblast cells (Tet-On-MyoD) do not differ from the wild-type cells in terms of morphology, proliferation rate, and gene expression without DOX treatment.
